lessons.title: Satire and the risk of misreading tone: A Modest Proposal
lessons.explanation: Satire works by adopting a voice it does not share, and its central risk is that a reader will take the voice at face value. Swift's A Modest Proposal is the standard case. Its opening sentence sounds like an earnest reformer: ‘It is a melancholy object to those, who walk through this great town, or travel in the country, when they see the streets, the roads, and cabbin-doors crowded with beggars of the female sex, followed by three, four, or six children, all in rags, and importuning every passenger for an alms.’ The distress is real, and the proposal that follows is that the poor should sell their children as food, with the pricing worked out in detail: ‘I have reckoned upon a medium, that a child just born will weigh 12 pounds, and in a solar year, if tolerably nursed, encreaseth to 28 pounds’, and ‘ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child’, against a nursing cost of ‘the value of two shillings’, so that ‘the mother will have eight shillings neat profit’. Nothing in the pamphlet announces that the speaker is not Swift. The reader has to earn that conclusion by finding the norm against which the proposal is outrageous — which is why satire is the genre where misreading tone has consequences [1].
lessons.example: Run the four tests for ironic tone on the proposal's most famous paragraph. Step one, paraphrase literally: the author advocates infanticide as a solution to poverty, dress the meat, and reserve ‘twenty thousand’ children ‘for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males’. Step two, coherence: does the literal reading make the pamphlet's other sentences work? It does not. The proposal claims to aim at ‘relieving the poor’, yet its remedy multiplies the harm; it explains its reasoning by analogy with livestock — ‘which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine’ — and that analogy is the joke rather than the argument. Step three, entitlement and self-incrimination: the speaker says what no honest projector would say, offering ‘ten shillings for the carcass’ as a benefit to tenants, and his sharpest sentence is an admission disguised as praise — landlords ‘as they have already devoured most of the parents, seem to have the best title to the children’. That word ‘devoured’ is the hinge: the pamphlet literalises a metaphor that rent and absent landlordism had already made true, so the cannibalism it proposes is a figure for a cannibalism already in operation. Step four, evidence of the frame: the closing paragraphs insist the author has no private gain — ‘I have no children, by which I can propose to get a single penny; the youngest being nine years old, and my wife past child-bearing’ — and the disinterestedness is the final irony, since the persona's only conceivable motive, profit, is withdrawn. A counterreading deserves statement: a reader could argue that the pamphlet's contempt extends to the Irish poor themselves, since the persona treats them as cattle. The evidence cuts the other way at the hinge sentence about landlords, and the strongest formulation is therefore bounded: the primary target is a policy and a mentality that convert persons into commodities, and the persona's contempt is a device for exhibiting that conversion [1][2].
lessons.question: Which feature of A Modest Proposal is the strongest internal evidence that its speaker is a satiric persona rather than the author's own voice?
lessons.answer: The proposal's own logic contradicts its stated aim of relieving the poor, and its closing disclaimer removes the only motive a sincere projector could have
lessons.distractor: The proposal is exaggerated, and exaggeration is the sign of a joke
lessons.correction: Exaggeration alone is not decisive: a reformer can exaggerate a remedy in earnest. What settles the question is internal incoherence between the stated aim and the means, together with the removal of the speaker's interest. Ask whether the literal reading can account for the text's own sentences.

depth.definitions: Satire ridicules conduct or institutions in order to correct them, and it typically employs irony, in which a speaker's meaning differs from the literal sense of the words. A persona is the constructed speaker of a text, distinct from the author, and free indirect discourse from lesson 33 prepares the vocabulary for its analysis. Tone is the speaker's attitude as inferred from diction and arrangement. Juvenalian satire is harsh and indignant, Horatian satire amused and urbane, and the distinction is a spectrum rather than a taxonomy. The implied author names the norm-governed construct a reader infers from the whole work, which is what makes an ironic reading available. Prerequisites: irony and its evidence standard from lesson 35, and the interest-versus-falsehood distinction from lesson 34 [2][3].
depth.mechanism: Satire raises three specific risks, and each has a diagnostic. The first is literalisation, where a reader cannot find the norm and acts on the proposal; diagnose it by asking what the literal reading must do with sentences that contradict its own aim. The second is co-option, where a hostile or careless reader detaches the persona's words from the work's norm and reuses them sincerely; the defence is internal, since the text's own contradictions mark the gap, so a careful reader can point at the hinge sentence where the metaphor is literalised. The third is flattening, where an ironic reading cancels all moral seriousness, so the pamphlet becomes a cruel joke about the poor; diagnose that by asking what the literal reading explains better, and by identifying the target — a policy that treats persons as commodities — rather than the persons themselves. Underneath these risks lies a mechanism: satire argues by hypothetical consistency, taking a society's operative principles and following them to their conclusion. The proposal's arithmetic is that device in action, an orderly bookkeeping of human lives, and its orderliness is the indictment. One further check rewards care. The persona's own figures do not agree: one fourth of twenty thousand breeders is five thousand males to fifteen thousand females, which is one male to three females, not the ‘one male will be sufficient to serve four females’ asserted in the same paragraph. Its limits: an ironic reading must be argued from textual signals and not from a reader's confidence about the author's character; and the persona's voice can be more memorable than its target, which is what makes satire co-optable in practice [2][3].
depth.secondExample: Compare Swift's own later satire to see a different frame with a different risk. At the end of Gulliver's Travels the narrator reports, of his return to England, that ‘I began last week to permit my wife to sit at dinner’ and explains his horror at the human form, so that Gulliver's derangement is the joke and the norm is his lost judgement. In A Modest Proposal the persona is lucid, coherent and calm; in the Travels the narrator is lucid too, but increasingly deranged. The comparison yields a testable claim about how ironic frames are signalled: in the Travels the frame announces itself through pathology that the reader can diagnose, while in the Proposal every sentence could in principle appear in an authentic pamphlet of political arithmetic, and only the coherence test separates them. That is why the Proposal is the sharper lesson in tone: the reader has to do the work without help from a broken narrator, and the risk of misreading is correspondingly higher [1][3].
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first reads the pamphlet literally as advocacy and denounces the author, which fails the coherence test and mistakes a persona for a person. The second says the piece is only a joke and so rescinds its argument, missing the hinge sentence about landlords and the consistent target of policy. The third applies the word ‘irony’ to any statement it finds unpleasant, without naming a norm; irony needs the norm stated and the textual pressure quoted, or it is just a mood label. The fourth treats the historical target as closed, so the pamphlet becomes an artefact about eighteenth-century Ireland with no transfer. The transferable question is whether some current arrangement converts a class of persons into an accounting line, and the proposed answer is testable by looking for the equivalent of ‘devoured most of the parents’ — a metaphor a system has already made literal [2][3].
depth.application: Choose three sentences from the pamphlet and write for each (a) a literal paraphrase and (b) the reading you would defend, with the norm named and the text's signal quoted. Then write 240–280 words on how the pamphlet's arithmetic works as an argument, including one calculation the persona makes and one computation of your own from the figures he gives. Self-review rubric: two points for genuinely distinct paraphrases; two for a named norm with quoted support; two for the calculation with numbers shown; two for a claim about what the arithmetic is doing; one for a stated falsification condition, such as a contemporary pamphlet that uses the same figures sincerely. Model direction: the strongest claim is that the persona's orderly bookkeeping — nursing cost two shillings against a sale price of ten — converts a moral horror into a margin, and the conversion is the target of the satire rather than its proposal.
depth.summary: Satire requires a reader to reconstruct a norm and then read the speaker against it, and A Modest Proposal is the hard case because the persona never breaks character. The tools are consistency, coherence, internal contradiction and the removal of self-interest; the risks are literalisation, co-option and the flattening that turns a moral argument into a cruel joke. Carry the habit of naming the target separately from the voice that attacks it, and of showing your arithmetic, since satiric argument is often quantitative and its numbers can be checked.

lessons.title: Comparing two texts on a shared theme with evidence: the house with a hidden life in Jane Eyre and Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
lessons.explanation: Comparison is commonly taught as a list of similarities and differences, which produces two summaries standing side by side and no argument. A comparison becomes an argument when a single claim is made about both texts and each text supplies evidence the other cannot. Take a shared theme with a precise formulation: in both Jane Eyre and Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, a respectable house contains a section that hides a life, and in both an ordinary explanation is offered that is true but insufficient. Jane Eyre supplies the pattern in three sentences. Jane explores Thornfield and finds a passage that ‘separating the front and back rooms of the third storey’ is ‘narrow, low, and dim, with only one little window at the far end, and looking, with its two rows of small black doors all shut, like a corridor in some Bluebeard's castle’; she hears a laugh that is ‘curious ... distinct, formal, mirthless’; and when she asks about it, Mrs Fairfax answers, ‘Some of the servants, very likely ... perhaps Grace Poole.’ Jekyll and Hyde supplies the same structure in architectural form: at one point in a busy commercial street ‘a certain sinister block of building thrust forward its gable on the street. It was two storeys high; showed no window, nothing but a door on the lower storey and a blind forehead of discoloured wall on the upper’, and its door ‘was equipped with neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and distained’. Two houses, two hidden lives, two explanations that are true and useless [1][2].
lessons.example: Build the comparison in five steps, and keep the texts alternating rather than sequential. Step one, state one claim that covers both: domestic architecture is used to represent the division of a self or a household into a public front and a hidden occupant, and the hiding is achieved by the structure's own conventions — corridors, locked doors, unvisited rooms. Step two, match the evidence units so that each text answers the same question. Question: how is the threshold described? Jane Eyre: the passage's ‘two rows of small black doors all shut’. Jekyll and Hyde: the windowless façade with ‘nothing but a door on the lower storey’. Question: what sound or sign marks the hidden occupant? Jane Eyre: a laugh that is ‘distinct, formal, mirthless’. Jekyll and Hyde: footsteps and a door used at night, and Enfield's account of a small figure who trampled a child, of whom he says, ‘He must be deformed somewhere; he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn't specify the point’. Question: what ordinary explanation is offered? Jane Eyre: ‘perhaps Grace Poole’. Jekyll and Hyde: the lawyer's assumption that a disreputable man has some hold over a respectable one. Question: how adequate is the explanation? In both cases it is literally true — Grace Poole is the person heard, and Hyde does have a door — and in both cases it accounts for the facts while missing the meaning. Step three, name the difference that matters, because a comparison with no difference is a repetition. In Brontë the hidden life is a housed woman whose condition the plot eventually reveals to be the consequence of a colonial marriage and a family's confinement of the mentally ill; the revelation distributes blame onto a system of property and marriage. In Stevenson the hidden life is the same person as the householder, so secrecy protects not another body but a second self, and the blame falls inward. Step four, state what would falsify the claim: if one text's explanation turned out to be complete and adequate, the shared pattern would collapse at that point, leaving a difference rather than a similarity. Step five, price a counterreading: one may object that the parallel is a genre commonplace — Gothic houses always hide something — and the answer is that the claim's substance lies in the parallel inadequacy of the explanations rather than in the presence of a hidden room, which is why Gothic houses without a plausible, insufficient explanation do not produce the same effect [1][2][3].
lessons.question: What makes the comparison of the two houses a claim rather than a list of similarities?
lessons.answer: It asserts one thing about both texts — that a respectable house hides a life and offers an explanation that is true but insufficient — and names a difference in where the blame falls
lessons.distractor: It observes that Gothic novels often have locked rooms, which both texts share
lessons.correction: A shared genre convention is a description of a tradition, not a claim about these two works, and it predicts nothing. The argumentative comparison specifies a mechanism (the house as a division) and a consequence (where blame is assigned), and it states what would falsify it.

depth.definitions: A comparative claim asserts something about two or more texts that neither text can establish alone; a similarity list simply reports overlapping features. A theme is a recurring concern rather than a moral, and stating a theme is not yet an argument. An evidence unit is a matched feature — threshold, hidden occupant, explanation, adequacy of explanation — compared like for like. Warrant is the reasoning that connects evidence to claim. A falsification condition states what evidence would defeat a claim. Prerequisites: setting as argument from lesson 39, form and constraint from lesson 41, unreliable narration from lesson 45, and the frame-level vocabulary from lesson 34, since the two novels deliver their evidence through very different narrative arrangements, one a retrospective first-person account and the other a chain of documents ending in a confession [3].
depth.mechanism: Comparative argument works by four operations. Selection reduces the two texts to features that both can be asked about, which is why the questions must be formulated before the evidence is gathered. Alternation presents evidence from each text in turn under the same heading, which prevents serial summary and exposes asymmetry. Difference assignment asks what each text does that the other cannot, since a comparison without a difference has no explanatory purchase. Testing then attempts to falsify: look for a passage in either text that fits the claim badly, and report it. Two limits matter. The compared features may look alike while functioning differently because the narrative arrangements differ, so a comparison of a first-person retrospective novel with a documentary one must adjust for who can know what. And over-generalisation is the standing hazard, since any two nineteenth-century novels will share themes if the themes are stated loosely enough, which is why a claim should be narrow enough that a reader could name a text it would fail on [3].
depth.secondExample: Test the same method on a harder theme to see where comparisons fail: the feeling of being watched unseen. In Jane Eyre the watcher is an inhabitant of the house whose presence is signalled by sound, and the concealment is maintained by the household's own arrangements — a servant given an explanation and a locked door given a story. In Jekyll and Hyde the watched figure is the householder himself as seen through others' accounts, and the concealment is maintained by documents, keys and wills; Utterson's approach is above all evidentiary, since he seeks the will, the handwriting and the handwriting's match. So the theme of concealment resolves into two different mechanisms, one of surveillance inside a house and one of documentation inside a professional world. The comparison now has a claim with a difference attached: secrecy in Brontë is maintained by a household's willingness not to ask, and in Stevenson by a professional class capable of asking but not of believing. This sharper version predicts where each novel will place its crisis — in a confrontation between persons for the first, in a legal and documentary unmasking for the second — and predictions of that kind are what a comparative claim is for [1][2].
depth.mistake: Four errors dominate essays of this kind. The first writes two mini-essays with a connective paragraph, which is comparison as juxtaposition; diagnose it by checking whether every paragraph contains both texts. The second states a theme as the thesis — ‘both novels explore duality’ — which is a topic, not a claim, and predicts nothing; repair it by specifying a mechanism and a consequence. The third picks features for convenience rather than for comparability, so a novel's plot detail is set beside another's imagery, and the comparison collapses because the units do not match. The fourth ignores the difference in narrative arrangement, reading a confessional document as though it carried the authority of a retrospective narration; state who narrates and what each narrator can know before comparing what they report [3].
depth.application: Choose a theme you can formulate in one sentence about two of the texts in this level. Build a four-column table — question asked, evidence from text A, evidence from text B, difference that remains — with at least three question rows. Then write 260–300 words presenting the comparative claim, with a matched pair of quotations, the difference named, one counterreading and one falsification condition. Self-review rubric: two points for a claim specific enough to fail on some text; two for matched evidence units; two for an explicit difference with consequences; two for quotations located accurately in named editions; two for a counterreading and a falsification condition. Model direction: the strongest comparative claims name a mechanism both texts use and a consequence each text draws differently, as with the household's willingness not to ask against the professional's inability to believe.
depth.summary: Comparison is an argumentative form: state one claim about both texts, match the evidence units, name the difference that the similarity leaves over, and give the claim a way to fail. Comparing Jane Eyre with Jekyll and Hyde shows the method earning its keep, because the houses look alike while the mechanisms of secrecy and the distribution of blame differ. Carry the four-column table into any comparative task, from examination essays to policy options, and remember that alternation is what keeps a comparison from becoming two summaries in a coat.

Note that the laugh's explanation is supplied by a character and that the narration does not contradict it openly; the reader must notice the gap. Public domain in the USA.

visual.title: Four-column comparison
visual.description: Matching evidence units across two texts, then naming the difference that remains, so the comparison argues rather than lists.
steps: Question 1 — the threshold: Jane Eyre's ‘two rows of small black doors all shut’ against Hyde's windowless façade with ‘nothing but a door’
Question 2 — the sign of the hidden occupant: a laugh ‘distinct, formal, mirthless’ against a small figure and a night door
Question 3 — the explanation offered: ‘perhaps Grace Poole’ against a respectable man's disreputable acquaintance
Question 4 — adequacy: both explanations are true and insufficient, which is the shared pattern
Difference that remains: the hidden life is another person in Brontë and the same person in Stevenson
Consequence: blame falls on property and marriage in one text, inward in the other
Test: if either explanation were adequate, the claimed similarity would collapse into a difference

lessons.title: Writing a sustained interpretive essay: thesis, counterargument and falsification
lessons.explanation: An interpretive essay is an argument about a text, and an argument has a shape: a claim, reasons that support it, evidence that can be located, a serious rival reading, and a statement of what would change your mind. The difference between a topic and a thesis is the difference between a subject and a position. ‘Responsibility in Macbeth’ is a topic; it can be developed in any direction and predicts nothing. A thesis reads like this: ‘Macbeth is responsible for Duncan's murder because Act 1 stages the moment at which his alternative policy of waiting becomes unavailable, and after that moment his soliloquies report decision rather than deliberation; the witches' prophecy is a condition of his action, not its cause.’ That sentence names a claim, a piece of the play, an evidentiary kind (the soliloquies), a counter-position (prophecy as cause) and an implicit concession. It is also vulnerable: a reader can point to the prophecy's literal fulfilment and argue that the play rigs the outcome, and that reader is doing exactly what the essay invites. A sustained essay is not longer because it repeats; it is longer because it does four additional jobs — establishing the problem and terms, working the evidence scene by scene, meeting the strongest objection, and setting limits on what the evidence can support [1][2][3].
lessons.example: Work the counterargument paragraph itself, because it is where most essays collapse. Weak version: ‘Some might say Macbeth was fated, but I think he chose.’ That sentence costs nothing, cites nothing and can be answered by anyone. Strong version proceeds in five moves. Move one, state the rival claim at full strength: the Weird Sisters' predictions are all fulfilled in the plot, and the final battle turns on riddling assurances (‘none of woman born’) that Macbeth misreads, so the play makes prophecy the engine of events. Move two, give the rival its best evidence with locations: the prophecy of kingship is realised, Birnam Wood moves, and Macbeth dies at the hands of a man not born of woman, which means the plot confirms the supernatural rather than testing it. Move three, say what follows if the rival is right: arguing about Macbeth's choices would be an error, because his deliberation would be the mere appearance of agency inside a predetermined script. Move four, answer with evidence that the rival must accommodate rather than ignore: Banquo hears the same prophecy, treats it as a warning — ‘The instruments of darkness tell us truths’ — and is not moved to kill; Macbeth abandons an available policy (‘If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me, / Without my stir’) only after Duncan names Malcolm his heir, which is a decision with a date; and his own soliloquy concedes that the motive is wanting itself, ‘Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself’. Move five, concede what the rival gets right and bound your claim accordingly: the play does fulfil its prophecies, so the defensible claim is that Macbeth's responsibility is neither denied nor diminished by them but exercised, since the fate is fulfilled through choices the play stages. A paragraph of that kind has done more than a summary of five scenes, and it can be attacked at named points, which is what makes it an argument [1][2].
lessons.question: What distinguishes a strong counterargument paragraph from a weak one in an interpretive essay?
lessons.answer: It states the rival reading at full strength with its best evidence, says what would follow if it were correct, answers it with locatable evidence, and concedes what it gets right
lessons.distractor: It mentions an opposing view briefly so that the essay can show it has considered both sides
lessons.correction: Mentioning an opposing view without evidence or consequence is decoration: it costs the argument nothing and cannot be tested. The strong version supplies the rival's best case, its implications, a specific answer and an explicit concession, so a reader can see exactly where the disagreement lies.

depth.definitions: A thesis is a contestable claim about a text; a topic is a subject. A warrant is the reasoning connecting evidence to claim, and without it a quotation is an ornament. A counterargument is the strongest version of a rival reading, a concession is the part of it your claim must grant, and a rebuttal is your answer to the rest. A falsification condition states what evidence would defeat your claim. Textual criticism supplies the edition problem: quotations must match the text actually cited. Secondary sources are arguments to be tested rather than authorities to be cited. Prerequisites: the claim-evidence-warrant-counterreading-falsification sequence from lesson 40, quotation discipline from lesson 41, and the genre-specific tools of this level [1][4].
depth.mechanism: An essay works because each paragraph performs one operation in a chain. The topic sentence states a sub-claim rather than a fact, so it commits the writer to something. Evidence arrives as a quotation with a location, kept short enough that the reader can see the words being argued about rather than trusting the essayist's summary. The warrant explains why those words support the sub-claim, which is where most student essays thin out, since a quotation followed by a generalisation leaves the inference unstated. The transition names the consequence, so the next paragraph inherits a problem rather than a topic. Every paragraph should survive the question ‘so what?’, and any paragraph that answers only ‘because this is interesting’ should be cut. Two limits govern the whole. First, textual: an argument about punctuation, metre or rhyme must declare its edition, and an argument that rests on a variant reading should say so. Second, evidentiary: interpretive claims about fictional persons are not psychological findings, and claims about the author's intention require external evidence, which is why attribution to a narrator or persona is part of the argument rather than a preliminary [3][4].
depth.secondExample: Apply the same architecture to a text of a different kind to see that it is not a formula for novels alone. A thesis about A Modest Proposal: ‘The pamphlet's target is not the poor but the accounting that converts them into a line of profit, and its evidence is the arithmetic itself: a nursing cost of two shillings against a sale price of ten, with the difference described as “neat profit”.’ The evidence is quotable, the warrant explains that a margin is what the persona is calculating, and the counterargument has a real rival — that the satire's contempt falls on the Irish poor — which must then be met with the hinge sentence about landlords who ‘have already devoured most of the parents’. The falsification condition is specific: a contemporary pamphlet that uses the same figures in good faith would show that the arithmetic alone is not the signal, and the argument would have to rest on contradiction instead. The same skeleton — claim, located evidence, warrant, rival, condition — organises an argument about a poem, a play, a novella or a pamphlet, and the only thing that changes is the kind of evidence available [2][4].
depth.mistake: Four errors are standard. The survey essay summarises the text and then appends its meaning; diagnose it by checking whether each paragraph makes a claim a reader could deny, and if every sentence is true and uncontested, the essay has no thesis. The unfalsifiable thesis is one no evidence could defeat — ‘the novel explores the complexity of human nature’ — which should be rewritten until a counterexample is imaginable. The decorative counterargument mentions opposition so the essay can appear balanced; apply the cost test, and if the counterargument does not force a concession, replace it with a stronger one. The decorated quotation appends a line without a warrant; repair it by writing the sentence that begins ‘this matters because’. A fifth error is quoting an edition you did not read, which turns a small slip into an unverifiable claim, and the remedy is to quote exactly what the linked text prints and to say so when editions differ [1][3].
depth.application: Capstone task: write a 900–1,200 word interpretive essay on one text from this level. Requirements: a thesis specific enough to fail on some reading; at least four quotations with chapter, scene or line locations from named editions; a warrant sentence after each quotation; one counterargument stating the strongest rival case with its best evidence; one explicit concession; one paragraph on the limits of your evidence, including any edition or performance variation; and one sentence stating what would change your mind. Self-review rubric: three points for a contestable thesis; three for located evidence with warrants; three for a counterargument that costs the thesis something; two for stated limits; two for structure in which every paragraph advances the claim. Model direction: choose the claim you can barely defend rather than the one everyone already believes, and let the last paragraph say what remains unresolved, since a conclusion that resolves everything has usually stopped reading.
depth.summary: A sustained interpretive essay is a chain of contestable claims, each supported by located evidence and an explicit warrant, tested against the strongest rival reading and bounded by stated limits. The sequence never changes — claim, evidence, warrant, counterargument, concession, falsification condition — while the kind of evidence does. Writing this way forces the reader's intellectual honesty into the open: you must say what would change your mind, and in saying it you show what your argument rests on.

visual.title: The architecture of a sustained argument
visual.description: One thesis carried through evidence, warrant, counterargument, concession and falsification condition, with each paragraph performing a single operation.
steps: Thesis: a claim that names a moment in the text, an evidentiary kind and a rival position
Paragraph operation: sub-claim, then short located quotation, then the warrant sentence beginning ‘this matters because’
Counterargument at full strength: prophecy fulfilled, Birnam Wood, ‘none of woman born’
Consequence: if prophecy drives events, deliberation would be the appearance of agency
Rebuttal with evidence: Banquo resists the same prophecy; the waiting policy is abandoned only after Malcolm is named heir
Concession: the play does fulfil its prophecies, so the claim is bounded to responsibility exercised through them
Limits and exit: name edition variation, and state what would change your mind

questions.prompt: A student objects that a story about an unremarkable clergyman cannot carry moral weight. Which response best follows Eliot's practice in ‘Amos Barton’?
questions.answer: The moral weight is carried by selected particulars — a grave, a child's silent grip, a contrast with a wealthy visitor — which make an ordinary life visible rather than by a heroic subject
questions.distractor: Weight comes from the narrator's commentary, which tells the reader what to feel about ordinary people
questions.correction: Commentary is the weakest instrument in the passage: the burial scene withholds judgement and the detail does the work. The narrator's programme is an argument with an agenda, while the particulars are what a reader can check.

questions.prompt: An essay claims Jane Eyre forms herself through choices alone. Which evidence in the novel most complicates that claim?
questions.answer: The inheritance and the fire remove obstacles and change Rochester's condition, so the settlement depends partly on arrangement rather than on Jane's decisions
questions.distractor: Jane refuses Rochester, which shows that her choices have real costs and therefore real agency
questions.correction: The refusal shows agency exists; it does not show that agency alone produced the ending. A claim about self-formation must account for the plot's coincidences, which the narration reports without explaining.

questions.prompt: A reader insists A Modest Proposal is simply a cruel joke with no target. Which evidence best answers the reader?
questions.answer: The proposal's own logic contradicts its stated aim of relieving the poor, and the sentence about landlords who ‘have already devoured most of the parents’ marks the policy the pamphlet attacks
questions.distractor: The proposal is exaggerated beyond belief, which shows that the author cannot have meant it
questions.correction: Unbelievability proves nothing on its own; the argument is internal. The contradiction between aim and means, plus the metaphor of devouring, identifies the target as a system that converts persons into commodities.

questions.prompt: A draft compares two novels by devoting one paragraph to each and a third to the observation that both are Gothic. What repair does the lesson require?
questions.answer: Recast it as one claim about both texts with matched evidence units and a named difference in mechanism or consequence
questions.distractor: Add a fourth paragraph listing further similarities so that the comparison is more complete
questions.correction: More similarities produce a longer list, not an argument. Comparison requires the same questions asked of both texts and a difference that reports what each text does which the other cannot, with a falsification condition.

questions.prompt: An essay includes the paragraph ‘Some readers think Macbeth was fated, but I believe he chose freely.’ What must be added?
questions.answer: The rival reading at full strength with its best evidence, its implications if true, a located rebuttal, and an explicit concession of what it gets right
questions.distractor: A quotation from the play to demonstrate that fate is a theme the essay has noticed
questions.correction: A quotation without a warrant and a rival stated as a rumour are both decoration. The counterargument must carry the rival's evidence and force the thesis to adjust, or the essay has not engaged the strongest objection.

questions.prompt: Two essays read the same sonnet. One interprets its argument without mentioning form; the other marks the octave and sestet and argues that the turn is where the poem hands its question to another speaker. Which reading is stronger, and why?
questions.answer: The formal reading, because it locates the change of speaker at a point the rhyme scheme independently marks, and it states what the opposite reading must explain
questions.distractor: The thematic reading, because arguments belong to meaning while line-endings belong to technique
questions.correction: Technique is meaning when a division is what licenses the shift of voice: the sestet's new rhyme pattern and the reply from ‘patience’ coincide, so the formal observation is evidence. The thematic reading is not wrong, only thinner, unless it can account for the placement.

questions.prompt: An essay asserts that Macbeth is a tragedy of a fatal flaw, that hamartia means a character defect, and that the play therefore teaches a moral lesson. Which revision is required?
questions.answer: Hamartia is a contested term, rendered by Butcher as ‘some error or frailty’ rather than vice, and the play's evidence is better described as a staged choice with a visible alternative
questions.distractor: The essay should replace the word hamartia with catastrophe, since the play's ending is catastrophic
questions.correction: The problem is the equation of a translated term with a settled doctrine. Aristotle's criteria describe the plays he knew, so the essay should argue the transfer and point to the scene where a rival path is visible, as Banquo's resistance supplies.

questions.prompt: A reader argues that Twelfth Night cannot be cruel to Malvolio because the play ends with music, marriages and the Duke's order to ‘entreat him to a peace’. Which cumulative objection applies?
questions.answer: The ending is a convention and a promise of repair that arrives after the victim's exit, so the reading must explain why the play supplies the language of abuse and withholds reintegration
questions.distractor: The objection fails because comedies always reconcile their antagonists, which is what the marriages demonstrate
questions.correction: A convention cannot answer a question about a particular play's allocations. Count who gains, who pays and who is present at the close; the comedy's own words — ‘most notoriously abus'd’ — then become evidence rather than atmosphere.

questions.prompt: A draft claims the windowless façade in Jekyll and Hyde proves that the building is supernatural. Which correction follows the level's standards for symbolic and uncanny reading?
questions.answer: The description is an ordinary architectural fact whose explanation is withheld, and the uncanny effect is produced by that withholding rather than proving anything beyond the ordinary
questions.distractor: The façade is a symbol of Jekyll's sin, and symbols in Gothic fiction are always supernatural in reference
questions.correction: Both claims outrun the evidence. Locate the literal function first — a windowless service building with a disused door on a commercial street — then describe the effect and argue for any moral mapping with a warrant and a falsification condition.

questions.prompt: Two critics disagree about the governess in The Turn of the Screw: one says the text signals her unreliability, the other that the reader's norms produce it. Which procedure gives the dispute a checkable shape?
questions.answer: Name the criterion being used — contradiction, inference beyond evidence, missing corroboration, shaping rhetoric or framing — then state what evidence would settle it and treat the two approaches as rival norms
questions.distractor: Appeal to the author's stated intention in a preface, since the author decides what the text means
questions.correction: Intention is external evidence and does not settle the reading of a published text; the approaches differ about where norms live, so the productive move is to declare the norm and test the account against it, keeping the question of what happened separate from the question of warranted inference.

questions.prompt: An essay quotes a narrator's defence of commonplace subjects as proof that the novel values ordinary lives, then ignores a passage in which the same narrator mocks a character. What cumulative repair is needed?
questions.answer: Attribute the programme to its narrator, then test the practice against the programme, since the same voice can argue for sympathy and condescend to a character it describes
questions.distractor: Delete the mockery passage, because a narrator's stated programme is the text's position
questions.correction: Deleting evidence is the error, not the repair. Narrator and text are distinct, and the strongest reading reports both the argument and the practice and asks what the discrepancy shows. That is also the method for distinguishing interior report from generalisation.

questions.prompt: A student claims a novel's protagonist ‘grows into herself’ because the chapters follow her from childhood to marriage. Which requirement does the claim fail?
questions.answer: It substitutes sequence for a claim about a capacity tested under cost, and it ignores that a retrospective narrator selects the episodes that make the arc look inevitable
questions.distractor: It relies on chapters rather than on scenes, and only scenes can show development
questions.correction: The problem is not the unit of evidence but the absence of a stated change, a test and a cost. Add the before-and-after comparison and note the teller's shaping, then the arc becomes a claim a reader could contest.

questions.prompt: An essay about A Modest Proposal states that the pamphlet's figures show the author's contempt for the poor. Which additional step would make the argument responsible?
questions.answer: Compute the persona's arithmetic from the figures he gives, then show what the bookkeeping does to persons, and treat contempt for the poor as a rival reading to be met with the landlords sentence
questions.distractor: Quote the most shocking sentence, since the strongest evidence of contempt is the proposal to eat children
questions.correction: Shock is not analysis, and the arithmetic is checkable: twenty thousand reserved for breed leaves one hundred thousand for sale, and a two-shilling cost against a ten-shilling price is a margin. Showing what the calculation performs locates the target before the reading assigns contempt.

questions.prompt: Two texts are compared because both contain a hidden room. Which reformulation turns the observation into an argument?
questions.answer: A single claim about how each text uses domestic architecture to divide a public front from a hidden life, with matched evidence units and a named difference in where blame falls
questions.distractor: A claim that Gothic fiction uses hidden rooms to generate suspense, illustrated from both texts
questions.correction: A genre generalisation is a description of a tradition and predicts nothing about these two works. The argumentative version asks the same questions of each text, names the surviving difference and states what would falsify the claim.

questions.prompt: A thesis reads: ‘This play explores the complexity of human nature and the ambiguity of moral choice.’ Which diagnosis and repair apply?
questions.answer: The thesis is unfalsifiable, so it should be rewritten until a competing reading could defeat it, naming a moment, an evidentiary kind and a rival position
questions.distractor: The thesis is acceptable because ambiguous works generate ambiguous theses
questions.correction: A claim that no evidence could refute cannot be argued with, which is the test applied throughout this level to irony, symbol and unreliability alike. Specify the scene, the evidence and the opposing reading, and add the condition under which you would withdraw.

questions.prompt: Task: build one claim that spans a verse passage and a prose passage from this level. Which plan meets the level's standard?
questions.answer: Quote both from named editions, state one claim both support, give a warrant for each piece of evidence, name the difference in what each passage can show, then add a counterreading and a falsification condition
questions.distractor: Quote both, summarise the techniques of each, and conclude that verse and prose represent experience in complementary ways
questions.correction: Summary and complementarity are not claims, and the comparison must show what each passage supplies that the other cannot — a formal constraint in one case, a selected detail in the other — with a stated falsification condition.

questions.prompt: A draft quotes a modernised sonnet reading ‘Ere half my days’ while citing a transcription that prints ‘E're half my days’, and uses the modernised line to support a metrical claim. What must be corrected, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Quote the edition actually cited or cite the edition quoted, then re-count the beats in that text, because metrical and formal claims are claims about a specific printing
questions.distractor: Standardise the quotation to modern spelling, since a metrical pattern is unaffected by accidentals
questions.correction: Spelling and punctuation affect syllable counts and line-division evidence, and a quotation detached from its source cannot be checked. This level pairs every formal claim with a named edition for that reason.
